Dr. Lee: Good to see you again, Mr. Alvarez. How have you been since your last visit?
Patient: Honestly, my sugars have been running high in the mornings, 180 to 210. I've been thirsty a lot and getting up at night to urinate.
Dr. Lee: Are you taking metformin 1000 mg twice a day as prescribed?
Patient: Yes, every day. I did miss lisinopril a couple of times last week.
Dr. Lee: Your blood pressure today is 148 over 92, heart rate 84. A1c from last week came back at 8.9%. Weight is up three pounds. Let's start you on empagliflozin 10 mg daily and increase lisinopril to 20 mg daily. I also want a basic metabolic panel and a urine microalbumin today. Please follow up in 6 weeks and we'll recheck A1c in 3 months. Let's also refer you to nutrition for a diabetes diet review.
Patient: Okay, sounds good.

encounters.raw_transcript:
Dr. Bhatt: Mr. Reyes, welcome back. You've been dealing with low back pain for a while now — remind me how long.

Patient: About six months. Maybe a little longer. It started after I helped my brother move a sofa, and it's never really gone away.

Dr. Bhatt: How would you describe the pain now?

Patient: It's a dull ache most of the time, mostly in my lower back on the right side. Sometimes it shoots down my right leg, almost to my knee. Sitting for a long time at work makes it worse. Lifting anything heavier than about fifteen pounds makes it worse. First thing in the morning it's stiff, but loosens up after I walk around.

Dr. Bhatt: Any numbness or tingling?

Patient: A little bit on the outside of my right calf, maybe. It comes and goes.

Dr. Bhatt: Any weakness — trouble lifting your foot, or knee buckling?

Patient: No.

Dr. Bhatt: Any problems with your bladder or bowels — incontinence, trouble urinating, numbness in the groin?

Patient: No, nothing like that.

Dr. Bhatt: Any unexplained weight loss, fevers, night sweats?

Patient: No.

Dr. Bhatt: Any history of cancer?

Patient: No.

Dr. Bhatt: Any IV drug use or recent infections?

Patient: No.

Dr. Bhatt: Good — no red flags. What have you tried so far?

Patient: Ibuprofen eight-hundred two or three times a day. That takes the edge off. Heating pad at night. I tried a chiropractor a couple of times — didn't really help. I've been trying to walk more, but the pain flares up sometimes.

Dr. Bhatt: Any physical therapy?

Patient: No, not yet.

Dr. Bhatt: Any history of stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or heart disease?

Patient: Mild acid reflux. I take omeprazole. Otherwise I'm pretty healthy.

Dr. Bhatt: Let's examine you. Stand up please. Range of motion — forward flexion you reach your mid-shin, which is a little reduced. Extension about ten degrees, with some pain reproduction on the right. Lateral flexion is symmetric. Let me palpate — tenderness over the right paraspinal muscles at L4-5 and L5-S1, no midline tenderness, no step-off. Straight leg raise on the right reproduces pain at about sixty degrees, radiating to the lateral calf. On the left it's negative. Sensation is intact to light touch in all dermatomes except mild decreased sensation over the right lateral calf and dorsum of the foot. Strength is five out of five throughout, including toe extension and plantarflexion. Reflexes symmetric. Femoral stretch test negative.

Patient: What do you think it is?

Dr. Bhatt: You have chronic low back pain with a likely L5 radiculopathy on the right. Classic disc-related pattern — the exam supports a right-sided L4-L5 disc bulge or herniation irritating the L5 nerve root. The good news is that your neurological exam is intact — no weakness, no red flags, no signs of cauda equina. Most people with this improve with conservative management over eight to twelve weeks. I don't think we need imaging today.

Patient: I was hoping for an MRI.

Dr. Bhatt: I understand. But in the absence of red flags — progressive weakness, saddle anesthesia, cancer history, trauma, bowel or bladder issues — MRI findings within the first six weeks often don't change management. About thirty percent of people your age have a disc bulge on MRI and no symptoms at all. If you're not significantly improved in six weeks, we'll order it. Here's what I'd like to do. First, ease off the ibuprofen — eight-hundred three times a day for six months is a lot of NSAID. Switch to naproxen five-hundred twice a day with food, and only for a two-week course. Take it with your omeprazole. We'll also add topical diclofenac gel four times a day. Second, physical therapy — I'm referring you for evaluation. Aim for twice a week for six weeks. They'll work on core stabilization, McKenzie extension exercises, nerve glides. Third, I'm not going to prescribe opioids or muscle relaxants long-term. We know from the literature those don't improve outcomes and have real risks. Fourth, work ergonomics — I'll write a note asking your employer for a sit-stand desk and a twenty-minute walking break every two hours. Fifth, if you continue to have significant symptoms at six weeks, we'll get the MRI and consider an epidural steroid injection. If at any point you develop weakness, bowel or bladder symptoms, or worsening numbness, that's an urgent call — ER or immediate referral. Follow-up with me in four weeks.

Patient: Can I keep running?

Dr. Bhatt: Tough question. For now, I'd say substitute brisk walking or swimming for running while we settle the nerve root down. Once you're better, gradually reintroduce running. The PT can help with that progression.

encounters.raw_transcript:
Dr. Monroe: Hi Aiden. And hi mom — nice to see you again. Aiden, you're eight now, right?

Patient's mother: Eight and a half, he'll correct you.

Dr. Monroe: Fair enough. So Aiden, how have you been feeling?

Aiden: Okay. I coughed a lot at recess yesterday.

Dr. Monroe: When you run around or play sports, do you ever feel like you can't catch your breath?

Aiden: Yeah. Especially at soccer. Sometimes I have to sit out.

Dr. Monroe: How often in the last month?

Aiden: A couple of times a week, maybe.

Dr. Monroe: Mom, how about nighttime cough or waking up wheezing?

Mother: He's been waking up coughing about three nights a week for the last month. It's worse when the grass gets cut next door. And we had a cold in the house two weeks ago — after that it really ramped up.

Dr. Monroe: How often does he use his albuterol inhaler?

Mother: He carries it to school. The nurse's log showed he used it four times last week. And at home probably twice a week.

Dr. Monroe: Is he using the controller — the low-dose fluticasone?

Mother: Honestly, we've been inconsistent. When he's feeling good we skip it. When he's having trouble we remember.

Dr. Monroe: I understand. Let me take a listen. Aiden, can you take some big deep breaths for me? Good. Again. Thank you. Mom, I'm hearing some mild end-expiratory wheezing bilaterally, more on the right. No retractions. Respiratory rate is twenty-two, which is fine for his age. Oxygen saturation is ninety-seven percent on room air. Peak flow in the office was one-eighty, and his personal best from last summer was two-forty, so he's at seventy-five percent of his best. That's yellow zone.

Mother: Is it bad?

Dr. Monroe: It means his asthma isn't well-controlled right now. Based on the nighttime symptoms, the activity limitation, and the albuterol use, I'd put him in the "not well-controlled" category. Let me outline a plan. First, he needs to be on daily controller therapy, every day — not just when symptoms come. I'm going to step him up from low-dose fluticasone to a combination inhaler, fluticasone-salmeterol one-hundred-fifty, one puff twice a day. He's old enough to use a dry powder inhaler, but I'd rather he stay on a metered-dose with spacer for now, because the data on pediatric delivery is better with spacers.

Mother: He has a spacer, but I don't know if he's using it right.

Dr. Monroe: Aiden, can you show me how you take your inhaler?

Aiden: Okay. Shake it. Put it on the spacer. Breathe out, then breathe in.

Dr. Monroe: Good. Couple of tweaks. After you put the spacer in your mouth and press the inhaler, I want you to take a slow deep breath for about five seconds, then hold it for ten. Count to ten silently. Then breathe out. And if mom says take two puffs, rinse between them — wait thirty seconds, then do the second puff the same way. After your controller inhaler, rinse your mouth with water and spit it out. That's important — reduces the risk of thrush. Let's practice. Here, I'll count for you. One, two, three, four, five — hold — one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Breathe out. Good.

Mother: What about his triggers?

Dr. Monroe: Grass pollen is a big one for him, based on last year's testing. Spring allergy season is coming. I'm going to continue his cetirizine five milligrams daily through May. Avoid mowing grass. Keep windows closed during high-pollen days. He can play soccer, but pretreat with two puffs of albuterol fifteen minutes before practice, and keep it with him on the sidelines. Second-hand smoke — anyone smoke in the house?

Mother: My partner smokes on the porch.

Dr. Monroe: Even porch-smoking clings to clothes and hair. I'd encourage a total change of clothes before coming inside. I'm going to update his asthma action plan. Green zone, no symptoms, peak flow above two-hundred: fluticasone-salmeterol twice daily, allergy med, no albuterol needed. Yellow zone, cough or wheeze or peak flow one-sixty to two-hundred: same controller plus albuterol two puffs every four hours as needed. If not improving in twenty-four hours, call me. Red zone, severe symptoms, peak flow under one-sixty, can't complete sentences, lips or fingers blue: albuterol every twenty minutes and come straight to the ER. I'll print the action plan and send copies to school and soccer. Let's also update his flu shot today if he hasn't had it.

Mother: He hasn't.

Dr. Monroe: We'll do that before you leave. Follow up in six weeks and I want a repeat peak flow check to confirm we've gotten him back to green.
